pedagogy.summary: Children compare which of two objects is heavier by HEFTING (holding one in each hand) and by using a two-pan balance, learning that weight is felt and measured, not seen — size and appearance do not reliably tell you mass. The balance settles cases hefting can't. Language: heavy/light, heavier than, lighter than. (At this stage 'mass' and 'weight' are used interchangeably.)
bestPractices: Heft first (hands as scales), then confirm with a balance
Deliberately pair a small heavy object with a big light one so size cannot decide it — this is what breaks the 'bigger = heavier' assumption
Read the balance as 'the side that goes DOWN is heavier'
Use full comparative sentences: 'the tin is heavier than the box'
Keep it practical with real objects; move to ordering three items by pairwise balance comparisons
keyRepresentations: The two-pan balance (canonical model of comparison)
commonMisconceptions: Bigger = heavier — judges mass by size or appearance
The taller/longer/fuller object is heavier (conflates mass with another attribute)
Misreads the balance — thinks the RAISED pan is the heavier side
Expects to order objects by weight just by looking

learn.summary: Young children (about 4-6) compare which of two objects is heavier, first by HEFTING (holding one object in each hand) and then by confirming with a two-pan balance. The central aim is to challenge the 'bigger = heavier' assumption by deliberately pairing a small heavy object with a big light one, so size stops being a reliable guide. Children read the balance as 'the side that goes DOWN is heavier', use full comparative language (heavier than / lighter than), and progress to ordering three objects by pairwise comparison. At this stage 'mass' and 'weight' are used interchangeably. The curriculum frames this as a practical activity with real materials; screen or picture activities can support balance-reading and prediction but cannot deliver the felt sense of weight (no haptics).

activities.title: Heft then balance: feel it, then confirm
feedback: If the child picks the larger object, invite them to heft the pair with eyes shut, then let the balance decide — evidence over appearance. Repeat with more small-heavy/big-light pairs so size is repeatedly wrong.

If the child reads the balance backwards (raised pan = heavier), model with a known heavy-vs-light pair so they watch the heavy side drop; say 'the heavier side pushes DOWN' and let them press a pan to feel it fall.
When correct, prompt the reasoning: 'This one is smaller but you said it's heavier — how can something small be heavy?'
activities.rationale: For this age the embodied experience of feeling a small object press down is intended to do the conceptual work of challenging 'bigger = heavier'; the balance then provides shared, visible evidence that overrides appearance. The curriculum frames comparison of mass as a practical activity with real materials, moving from feeling to a balance.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils are taught to compare, describe and solve practical problems for mass/weight [heavy/light, heavier than, lighter than] and to 'measure and begin to record' mass/weight; at this stage mass and weight are used interchangeably.

NCETM Year 1 mastery mass tasks move from feeling ('sort three items lightest to heaviest by feeling them') to a balance with items 'quite similar in mass', and probe balance-reasoning ('which is heavier?', 'if you added a car to the teddy what would happen to the scales?', true/false from a balance picture) — designed so appearance/feel is unreliable and balance evidence decides.
Measurement Big Ideas frame it as comparison and equivalence conducted as a practical activity with real materials.
learnerActions: Hold one object in each hand (heft) and say which feels heavier — try this with eyes shut so appearance can't guide the choice.

Pair a small heavy object (a metal weight or pebble) with a big light object (an empty plastic box or inflated balloon), checked beforehand on the balance so the small item really is heavier (a small pebble can be lighter than a large box). Predict which is heavier before touching.
Place both on a two-pan balance and watch which pan goes down; say 'the ____ is heavier than the ____' in a full sentence.
Repeat with several deliberately misleading pairs (e.g. big cushion vs small tin of beans), checked beforehand so the small item really is heavier, so that size is repeatedly the wrong guide.
Press gently on one pan with a hand to feel that pushing down harder on one side makes that pan go down, just as a heavier object does.
activities.intendedInsight: Weight is felt and measured, not seen — a small object can be heavier than a big one, and the balance settles cases your eyes cannot.

activities.title: Order three objects by weight
feedback: If the child orders by look or by trial-and-error grabbing, scaffold with pairwise balance comparisons ('heavier than this one? lighter than that one?'). Systematic seriation is not expected at this age — it consolidates with practice, so do not drill an ordering rule.
Praise reasoning that uses the balance evidence to justify each placement.
activities.rationale: Ordering by successive pairwise balancing extends direct comparison and reinforces that weight evidence, not appearance, decides order. Developmentally, systematic seriation emerges gradually, so the task is scaffolded rather than drilled.
sourceClaims: NCETM Year 1 mastery mass tasks move from feeling ('sort three items lightest to heaviest by feeling them') to a balance with items 'quite similar in mass', and probe balance-reasoning ('which is heavier?', 'if you added a car to the teddy what would happen to the scales?', true/false from a balance picture) — designed so appearance/feel is unreliable and balance evidence decides.
Measurement Big Ideas frame it as comparison and equivalence conducted as a practical activity with real materials.
learnerActions: Take three objects, including at least one small-heavy and one big-light item.
Compare them two at a time on the balance ('Is this heavier than that?'), using the balance outcome each time.
Arrange them lightest to heaviest based on the pairwise comparisons, not on how they look.
Describe the order aloud using 'heavier than' and 'lighter than'.
activities.intendedInsight: You can put objects in order of weight by comparing pairs, and the order may differ from what their sizes suggest.

activities.title: Virtual balance: predict then watch the beam tip (scaffold)
feedback: When a prediction is wrong, replay the beam tipping and point out which labelled side went down.
Use the misleading pairs to prompt: 'It looked bigger — why did the other side drop?'
activities.rationale: A predict-then-reveal virtual balance may support balance-reading, prediction and the size-vs-weight surprise. It is offered as a scaffold: a screen cannot deliver the physical heft that is how young children first feel that weight isn't size, so it should supplement, not replace, hands-on work. The outcome is designer-controlled, so the objects must be configured so the small item really is heavier.
sourceClaims: NCETM Year 1 mastery mass tasks move from feeling ('sort three items lightest to heaviest by feeling them') to a balance with items 'quite similar in mass', and probe balance-reasoning ('which is heavier?', 'if you added a car to the teddy what would happen to the scales?', true/false from a balance picture) — designed so appearance/feel is unreliable and balance evidence decides.
learnerActions: Drag a small metal cube and a big foam block onto the two pans of a virtual two-pan balance; the objects are configured so the small dense cube genuinely outweighs the larger light block.
Predict which side will drop before releasing.
Watch the beam tip to reveal that the small cube wins, with running 'heavier/lighter' labels appearing on each side.
Try a round of deliberately misleading pairs (big cushion vs small tin), again set so the small heavy item is actually heavier.
Switch to an order-three-objects mode that works by successive balancing.
activities.intendedInsight: Reading a balance (down = heavier) and predicting outcomes can be practised on screen, and in this set-up (where the small object is actually heavier) the small-cube-wins surprise reinforces that size alone is not a reliable guide to weight.

activities.title: Balance-picture check (recognition)
feedback: If a child names the raised side as heavier, return to a real or virtual balance and watch the heavier side drop.
For true/false items, ask the child to point to which pan is down to justify their answer.
activities.rationale: Picture-based items give clean checks of balance-reading and comparison. They check interpretation (recognition) and do not elicit the child's own physical comparison; hefting cannot be assessed from a picture, so use these to confirm interpretation alongside hands-on work rather than in place of it.
sourceClaims: NCETM Year 1 mastery mass tasks move from feeling ('sort three items lightest to heaviest by feeling them') to a balance with items 'quite similar in mass', and probe balance-reasoning ('which is heavier?', 'if you added a car to the teddy what would happen to the scales?', true/false from a balance picture) — designed so appearance/feel is unreliable and balance evidence decides.
learnerActions: Look at a picture of a two-pan balance and say which object is heavier (the side tipped down).
Order a set of objects lightest-to-heaviest from a series of balance pictures.
Match objects to the balance outcome they would produce.
Answer a true/false claim read from a balance picture (e.g. 'the teddy is heavier than the car').
activities.intendedInsight: Once the physical idea is in place, you can interpret balance pictures: the lower pan holds the heavier object.

constraints: The curriculum frames this as a practical activity with real objects in real hands: hefting a small heavy object and feeling it press down is the embodied experience intended to challenge 'bigger = heavier'. Screen and picture activities can point toward this but cannot supply the felt sense of weight (no haptics).

Deliberately include at least one small-heavy vs big-light pair, and ensure the chosen materials really do make the small item heavier — this mismatch is what makes size an unreliable guide; without it the activity can be solved by appearance alone.
Virtual-balance and balance-picture tasks are scaffolds for balance-reading and prediction; they do not assess or supply the felt sense of heft, so pair them with hands-on comparison.
Recognition-only picture tasks (choosing/matching) check interpretation but do not elicit the child's own physical comparison; do not rely on them as the only evidence of understanding.
Do not expect systematic ordering (seriation) of three objects at this age; scaffold with pairwise comparisons and let it consolidate with practice rather than drilling a rule.
Read the balance explicitly as 'the side that goes DOWN is heavier' (if the pans stay level, the objects weigh the same) and watch for the common reversal (thinking the raised pan is heavier).
Use full comparative sentences ('the tin is heavier than the box') rather than single words.
'Mass' and 'weight' are treated interchangeably at this stage; this is an age-appropriate simplification, not a claim that they are the same quantity.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row asserted a 3D balance 'adds nothing' over 2D and that a dialogue 'cannot' let a child heft or balance objects. These comparative/necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened: a 3D model and in-role dialogue simply offer different affordances and neither provides real heft; the genuine objective limit is that screens and pictures cannot deliver the felt sense of weight.

Efficacy wording was softened throughout (e.g. 'intended to', 'may support'): the pedagogical value of hefting and the virtual balance for this age is plausible and curriculum-aligned but not empirically validated here.

The virtual 'small cube wins' result is only true for suitably chosen sizes/densities; a large enough foam block could outweigh a tiny metal cube. Because the virtual balance is designer-controlled, the objects should be configured so the small item is genuinely heavier; for real objects, pick a clearly dense small item against a clearly light large item.
'Mass and weight used interchangeably' is a pedagogical simplification for ages 4-6; it is scientifically imprecise but appropriate here and flagged as such.

probeDeeper: 'This one is smaller but you said it's heavier — how can something small be heavy?'
'Here's a big cushion and a small tin of beans — which is heavier? How could you be SURE?' (a fresh big-light vs small-heavy case)
'When they're on the balance, how do you know which side is the heavier one?'
assess.correctAnswer: Hefts and reports the small metal object as heavier despite being smaller (it presses down); on the balance names the pan that goes DOWN as the heavier one; orders the three by weight (not by size), using 'heavier than / lighter than'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Judges the heavier object by size or appearance — 'the big box must be heavier because it's bigger'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Have them heft the pair with eyes shut, then let the balance settle it — evidence over appearance; repeat with several small-heavy / big-light pairs so size is repeatedly wrong.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 1 picks the larger object before or against hefting; discounts the balance when it contradicts size

errorPatterns.pattern: Misreads the balance — thinks the RAISED pan holds the heavier object
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model with a known heavy vs light pair so they watch the heavy side drop; 'the heavier side pushes DOWN'; let them press a pan to feel it fall.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 2 points to the higher side as heavier

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders three objects by grabbing / by size rather than by systematic pairwise comparison
errorPatterns.nextMove: Don't expect systematic seriation at this age; scaffold with pairwise balance comparisons ('heavier than this? lighter than that?') — it consolidates with practice, so don't drill an ordering rule.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 3 arranges by look or trial-and-error, not by comparing pairs on the balance

responseLevels.gap: Decides which is heavier by size or appearance; reads the balance backwards or ignores it.
responseLevels.full: Identifies the heavier object by heft and confirms with the balance (down = heavier) even when size misleads, orders three objects by mass, and can say that weight is not the same as size.
responseLevels.partial: Uses hefting or the balance for an obvious pair, but reverts to size when the objects look misleading, or reads the balance only with help.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a small heavy object (a metal weight or a pebble) and a large light object (a big empty plastic box or an inflated balloon), plus a third object, and a two-pan balance. Watch, don't quiz: (1) 'Hold one in each hand — which is heavier? How do you know?' (2) 'Now put them on the balance. Which is heavier? How can you tell from the scales?' (3) 'Put all three in order, lightest to heaviest.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The deliberately small-heavy vs big-light pairing IS the discriminator — a child relying on size says the big box is heavier, a child attending to weight says the metal object is; the balance item separately catches whether they read 'down = heavier'.
